source: ELEC0031 Topic 3, Silicon Growth and Fabrication (32 slides). Facts are paraphrased from the slides; slide = PDF page. Where a slide is wrong the fact teaches the correct statement and records the slide wording in "corrects".

unreadable.what: The I–V sketch labels reverse currents of −50 µA (Ge) and −20 µA (Si). These are illustrative figure values (real small-signal Si diodes leak nA or less), so they are not taught; the knee voltages are.
The four process photos carry tiny captions ("Seed Down", "Seed Pulling", "Shoulder"); they are legible only enlarged and are used as a sequence, not quoted.
The k0 table is a scanned image; Te (2.0×10⁻⁴), Li (1.0×10⁻²), Cu (4.0×10⁻⁴) and Au (2.5×10⁻⁵) are read but not taught, since none is a dopant used in the course.

The topic aims: course structure, nothing examinable.

facts.statement: The topic covers crystal structures; semiconductors, metals, insulators and doping; Czochralski and float-zone crystal growth; defects and point-defect modelling; and the chip fabrication process flow.
A crystal is characterised by a unit cell of dimension a (the distance between corner atoms) that repeats in x, y and z to fill all space.

The three basic cubic structures: simple cubic (atoms at the corners only), body-centred cubic, BCC (plus one atom at the cube centre) and face-centred cubic, FCC (plus one atom at the centre of each face).
Silicon has the diamond crystal structure: two merged FCC cells offset from each other by a/4 in x, y and z.
In the diamond-structure drawing every atom is bonded to four neighbours at the corners of a tetrahedron; the atoms of the second FCC cell sit inside the cube.
In silicon the nearest-neighbour (bond) distance is √3·a/4 ≈ 0.235 nm for a = 0.543 nm.
facts.corrects: The slide's ball-and-stick drawing labels a bond "0,15 nm": that is the C–C bond of diamond (carbon), not silicon.

facts.statement: Compound semiconductors share this kind of structure: binary (GaAs, AlP, AlAs, GaP, InSb, InP, InAs), ternary (AlGaAs, GaAsP) and quaternary (GaAlAsP).
The periodic-table extract: B, Al, Ga, In, Tl in group IIIA; C, Si, Ge, Sn, Pb in group IVA; N, P, As, Sb, Bi in group VA.
Miller indices (hkl) of a plane are the reciprocals of its intercepts with the x, y and z axes (in units of a), cleared to the smallest whole numbers.
Round brackets (hkl) name a plane; square brackets [hkl] name a direction.
A direction [hkl] is the vector with h, k and l units along x, y and z; in a cubic crystal [100] is perpendicular to the (100) plane.
Different planes have different atom densities: (111) is denser than (100).
In the figures (100) is a cube face cutting x at a, (110) cuts x and y at a and runs parallel to z, and (111) is the triangle cutting all three axes at a.
Electrons around an isolated atom occupy s, p, d and f orbitals, each with a characteristic shape.
An isolated atom has discrete energy levels, rising from 1s to 2s, 2p to 3s, 3p, 3d.
The electron cloud is the region around a nucleus where an electron will probably be: the "fuzzy" orbit of an atomic electron.
A solid is a collection of interacting atoms: the interaction turns each atomic level into a huge number of different levels.
Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons can occupy the same quantum state, which is why the shared levels must split.
facts.corrects: The slide says "no 2 electrons can have the same energy"; the principle forbids the same quantum state (two electrons of opposite spin share each level).

facts.statement: The discrete levels of isolated atoms split to form bands of energy states.
Each different set of atoms produces a unique set of bands.
In the figure, as the spacing d shrinks the atom levels fan out into an occupied band (top Ev) and an unoccupied band (bottom Ec) separated by the gap Eg.
At very large interatomic spacing (r = d) the atoms do not interact: the levels stay atomic.
At r = c the 3s and 3p electrons of neighbouring Si atoms start to interact and their energies start changing.
Between c and b each 3s or 3p level becomes a large number of closely packed levels.
At r = b the gap between the 3s and 3p bands disappears: the 8N levels are continuously distributed.
At the actual crystal spacing r = a, 4N filled levels are separated from 4N empty levels by the forbidden gap.
The lower, completely filled band is the valence band; the upper, empty band is the conduction band; the separation between them is the forbidden gap.
In the figure the inner levels 1s², 2s² and 2p⁶ stay sharp at the crystal spacing: only the outer 3s² 3p² levels form the bands.
Insulators have totally filled and totally empty bands, which allow no current (like liquid in a totally full or totally empty bottle), separated by a large gap.
In a metal the conduction band is only partly filled (half filled, or overlapping the valence band), so electrons can move.
Semiconductors have a smaller band gap than insulators and can be doped.
The figure: in a conductor the conduction and valence bands overlap; a semiconductor has a small gap; an insulator a large gap.
An intrinsic semiconductor (undoped, or i-type) is a pure semiconductor with no significant dopant present.
An extrinsic semiconductor has been doped; its dominant carrier concentration makes it n-type or p-type.
The band gap is Eg = Ec − Ev.
In the intrinsic diagram, electrons excited across the gap leave holes behind; the electron and hole distributions sit within about 2kBT of the band edges.
Under an electric field, conduction-band electrons and valence-band holes drift in opposite directions.
In n-type material a donor level ED sits just below Ec, and the conduction-band electron population is far larger than the valence-band hole population.
Doping is the deliberate, carefully predetermined introduction of specially chosen impurities.
Doping can increase the conductivity of a semiconductor by up to 8 orders of magnitude.
Group V atoms (P, As, Sb) are donors: easily ionised in Si, they provide extra conduction electrons, the majority carriers of n-type material.
facts.corrects: The slide lists "Group V atoms (B, P and As)": boron is in group III and is an acceptor.

facts.statement: Group III atoms (B, Al, Ga, In) are acceptors: easily ionised in Si, they provide extra holes, the majority carriers of p-type material.
Any holes in n-type material, or electrons in p-type material, are minority carriers.
Phosphorus is mainly used for n-type silicon processing; boron for p-type.
In the bond diagrams an As atom gives the n-type lattice an extra electron, and a Ga atom leaves the p-type lattice with a missing electron: a hole.
Near the junction the n side is depleted of electrons, exposing positive donor ions of concentration Nd; the p side exposes negative acceptor ions of concentration Na.
facts.corrects: The slide says the n side exposes "positive donor ions of concentration Na"; donor concentration is Nd.

facts.statement: In the figure M marks the metallurgical junction; the space-charge region extends Wp into the p side and Wn into the n side, with the field E0 pointing from n to p.
In the diode symbol the anode (A, +) is the p side and the cathode (K, −) the n side; conventional current flows from anode to cathode.
Forward current rises sharply above the "knee": about 0.7 V for silicon, 0.3 V for germanium.
In reverse bias only a small leakage current flows until the reverse breakdown voltage, where Zener or avalanche breakdown makes the current rise steeply.
A p-n junction is present in almost every semiconductor device.
Step 1: metallurgical-grade silicon (MGS) is made by heating silica with carbon; overall SiO₂ + 2C → Si + 2CO.
facts.corrects: The slide writes C + SiO₂ → Si(l) + CO₂(g): balanced, but at arc-furnace temperatures the carbon leaves as CO.

facts.statement: Step 2: MG silicon is purified by reacting it with HCl into the silicon-bearing gas trichlorosilane: Si + 3HCl → SiHCl₃ + H₂ + heat.
Step 3, the Siemens process: SiHCl₃ and hydrogen react to deposit pure polycrystalline silicon: 2SiHCl₃ + 2H₂ → 2Si + 6HCl.
Single-crystal silicon is grown from the polysilicon by two methods: Czochralski and float zone.
The raw Si for crystal growth is purified from SiO₂ (sand) by refining, fractional distillation and CVD.
The polysilicon contains < 1 ppb impurities, except oxygen (~10¹⁸ cm⁻³) and carbon (~10¹⁶ cm⁻³).
The polysilicon is melted and held close to 1415 °C, silicon's melting point, and a single-crystal seed starts the growth.
Pull rate, melt temperature and rotation rate are the important control parameters of Czochralski growth.
Essentially all silicon wafers used for ICs today come from Czochralski-grown crystals.
The puller cutaway: crystal puller and rotation mechanism, seed, single-crystal silicon, molten polysilicon in a quartz crucible, carbon heating element, heat shield and water jacket.
The photos: polysilicon chunks in the crucible; the seed is dipped into the melt (seed down), pulled into a thin neck (seed pulling), then widened into the shoulder.
A known amount of dopant is added to the melt to obtain the desired doping; boron and phosphorus are the most common p- and n-type dopants.
The equilibrium segregation coefficient is k0 = Cs/CL: the dopant concentration in the solid over that in the liquid.
Segregation coefficients in Si: B 0.8, P 0.35, As 0.3, Sb 0.023, Ga 0.008, Al 0.002, In 4×10⁻⁴, C 0.07, and O 1.25.
Most k0 < 1, so dopants prefer to stay in the liquid: as the crystal is pulled the melt gets richer in dopant and Cs increases.
In the puller schematic the seed holder turns one way (CCW) and the crucible the other (CW); argon flows in; RF coils heat a graphite susceptor holding the fused-silica crucible.
M0 is the initial melt weight, C0 the initial melt doping (dopant weight per gram of melt), S the dopant left in the melt and M the weight of crystal grown.
Growing dM of crystal removes −dS = Cs·dM of dopant from the melt.
The melt concentration is CL = S/(M0 − M).
With Cs = k0·CL these combine to dS/S = −k0·dM/(M0 − M).
Integrating from C0M0 gives Cs = k0·C0·(1 − M/M0)^(k0 − 1).
The first crystal to freeze (M = 0) has Cs = k0·C0.
facts.corrects: The slide says the composition starts "at K0M0"; it starts at k0·C0.

facts.statement: Cs increases continually along the ingot when k0 < 1 and decreases continually when k0 > 1.
The doping is most uniform for k0 close to 1, e.g. boron with k0 = 0.8.
The graph of Cs/C0 against fraction solidified: boron starts at 0.8 and stays near 1; P and As start near 0.3 and climb steeply at the end; Sb starts near 0.02.
The float-zone process is an alternative growth process that can be used for refining or for single-crystal growth.
In float zone, dopants and other impurities tend to stay in the liquid, so the moving zone refines the rod, especially with multiple passes.
Float zone: a polycrystalline rod held in chucks; a travelling RF coil melts a molten zone; single-crystal material grows above a seed below; inert gas flows through.
Crystal defects: vacancy (V), interstitial (I), dislocation, stacking fault (an extra plane of atoms) and precipitate.
Defects can exist in the crystal or be created by processing steps; in general they are detrimental to device processing.
Point defects (vacancies and interstitials) play a fundamental role in many process technologies.
An interstitial impurity is a foreign atom between lattice sites; in a compound lattice a missing ion is a cation or an anion vacancy.
The free energy of the crystal is minimised when a finite concentration of point defects exists.
In general CI0* ≠ CV0*, and both are strong functions of temperature.
Kinetics, rather than thermodynamics, may determine the defect concentration in a wafer.
Equilibrium interstitials: CI0* ≈ 1×10²⁷ exp(−3.8 eV/kT) cm⁻³.
Equilibrium vacancies: CV0* ≈ 9×10²³ exp(−2.6 eV/kT) cm⁻³.
These give CI0* and CV0* ≈ 0 at room temperature and 10¹²–10¹⁴ cm⁻³ at 1000 °C, too small to measure.
From ingot to wafers: the ingot is prepared for grinding, ground to diameter, then a flat is ground along it to mark the crystal orientation.
An internal-diameter wafer saw slices the ingot into wafers.
The finished wafer has a notch and a scribed identification number.
Sliced wafers are loaded into a carrier for batch processing in a chemical bath.
The wafer-fab flow: silicon wafer manufacture → epitaxial growth → oxidation → photolithography → etching, then diffusion or implantation, metallization, or packaging.
Oxidation, lithography and etching repeat for every layer: after diffusion/implantation the flow returns to epitaxy or oxidation, and after metallization to oxidation, until the chip is packaged.
Wafers arrive from the wafer manufacturer "epi-ready".
Epitaxial Si is grown by CVD at a high temperature, 950–1150 °C, for perfect crystallinity.
In CVD epitaxy, gas precursors (typically SiH₄) carry Si to the hot substrate and decompose on contact; the Si remains and the residual gases are pumped away.
Epitaxy is used for lightly doped layers on more heavily doped substrates.
CVD epitaxy operates below the Si melting point and needs an ultraclean surface, with in-situ cleaning.
The CVD diagram: transport to the surface, adsorption of the film precursor, surface diffusion and reactions, nucleation and island growth, step growth, and desorption of volatile products.
Molecular beam epitaxy (MBE) is an ultra-high-vacuum system with a background pressure of 10⁻¹¹ Torr.
RHEED gives in-situ monitoring of MBE growth.
The MBE growth rate is about 1000 nm per hour.
The MBE chamber: effusion cells aimed at the substrate, a RHEED gun, a mass spectrometer, an LN₂ cryopanel and the vacuum pump; new growth continues the substrate's crystal.
Thermal oxidation: Si + O₂ → SiO₂ (dry) and Si + 2H₂O → SiO₂ + 2H₂ (wet).
O₂ or H₂O diffuses through the existing SiO₂ and reacts with Si at the interface to form more SiO₂.
Forming 1 µm of SiO₂ consumes 0.44 µm of the Si substrate.
Dry oxidation (O₂) grows thin oxides, such as the gate oxide.
Wet oxidation (water) grows thick oxides.
Oxide growth slows as the oxide thickens (Deal–Grove model): thickness ∝ t at first, then ∝ √t.
Photoresists are polymer resins containing a photoactive (light-sensitive) compound and an alkaline-soluble resin.
Sensitivity to radiation (ultraviolet light) is the key property of materials used to image IC features.
Negative resists are hardened by the exposure light.
Positive resists are softened by the exposure light.
Developing dissolves the soluble resist: the exposed areas of a positive resist, or the unexposed areas of a negative resist.
facts.corrects: The slide says exposure "selectively polymerizes" the resist and develop "dissolves the unpolymerized resist": true of negative resists only. In positive resists the light breaks down the photoactive compound and the exposed resist dissolves.

facts.statement: Through the same mask, positive resist leaves a copy of the opaque pattern (an SiO₂ island after etching) and negative resist leaves its inverse (a window in the SiO₂).
Etches need high selectivity: HF solution attacks SiO₂ but not Si.
Isotropic (mainly chemical, wet) etching removes material sideways at about the same rate as downwards, undercutting the mask.
Undercut is insignificant for large features but becomes a serious problem when the feature size approaches the etch depth.
Anisotropic (mainly physical, e.g. sputtering) etching gives better pattern transfer and is used in all modern etch processes.
Anisotropic etching needs dry etching with plasmas, e.g. reactive ion etching (RIE), instead of liquid acids.
The etch figure: (a) a wide line with a curved undercut, (b) a narrow line almost cut through, (c) a line with vertical walls.
Predeposition introduces the dopant: 2B₂O₃ + 3Si → 3SiO₂ + 4B, or 2P₂O₅ + 5Si → 5SiO₂ + 4P.
Predeposition takes place in a quartz tube inside heating coils, with an inert carrier gas and the dopant flowing over the wafers.
Drive-in spreads out the doping profile.
Diffusion doping runs at 950–1200 °C.
D = D0·exp(−Q/kT), where D is the diffusion constant, Q the activation energy and T the temperature in K.
Through an oxide window the dopant spreads down and sideways under the oxide edge; the 10²¹, 10¹⁹ and 10¹⁶ cm⁻³ contours lie progressively deeper and wider.
Ion implantation: ions from an ion source are accelerated by a high voltage into a beam aimed at the Si wafer.
Ion energies range from about 1 keV to 200 keV.
The wafer is at room temperature during implantation.
After implantation a 900–1000 °C anneal is needed to activate the dopants and restore the Si crystallinity.
Implantation precisely controls the amount of dopant introduced and its depth below the surface.
Ion implanters are essential to modern IC manufacturing.
Metallization connects the fabricated devices together to perform circuit functions.
Thermal evaporation: a solid such as a pure metal is heated until it vaporises, then recondenses on a cooler substrate as a thin film.
The heating is done by passing a large current through a resistive filament container shaped as a basket, boat or crucible.
The filament material is chosen for the evaporation temperature and for its inertness to alloying or reaction with the evaporant.
In the evaporator the hot source sits inside a vacuum chamber with the substrates held above it, facing the metal vapour.
